items.text: Aim for one litter box per cat, plus one extra. So a home with one cat should ideally have two boxes.
items.attribution: Cornell Feline Health Center, Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine
items.sourceName: Choosing and Caring for Your New Cat

items.text: Most cats prefer simple litter boxes without hoods and unscented, fine-textured litter. Keep the box clean and change the litter frequently.
items.attribution: Cornell Feline Health Center, Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine
items.sourceName: Choosing and Caring for Your New Cat

items.text: Keep your cat's food and water dishes far away from the litter box to avoid contamination.
items.attribution: Cornell Feline Health Center, Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine
items.sourceName: Choosing and Caring for Your New Cat

items.text: A new cat should be examined by a veterinarian as soon as possible after coming home.
items.attribution: Cornell Feline Health Center, Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine
items.sourceName: Choosing and Caring for Your New Cat

items.text: Help your cat use a scratching post by rewarding it with treats, strokes and praise when it does.
items.attribution: Cornell Feline Health Center, Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine
items.sourceName: Choosing and Caring for Your New Cat

items.text: Dental disease is very common in older cats: studies report that between 50 and 90% of cats over four years of age have some form of it. Most forms are largely preventable or treatable with good preventive care.
items.attribution: Cornell Feline Health Center, Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine

items.text: The best way to prevent gingivitis in cats is to regularly remove plaque build-up by tooth brushing.
items.attribution: Cornell Feline Health Center, Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine

items.text: Use only tooth gel or toothpaste made specifically for cats. Human products can be toxic to cats.
items.attribution: Cornell Feline Health Center, Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine

items.text: Drooling, bad breath, bleeding where the gums meet the teeth, or reluctance to eat can be signs of dental disease. Mention them to your veterinarian.
items.attribution: Cornell Feline Health Center, Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine

items.text: Lilies are dangerous to cats: any exposure to leaves, bulbs, flowers, pollen or even the water the flowers sat in can cause acute kidney injury. If you suspect exposure, contact a veterinarian or the ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center right away.
items.attribution: ASPCA (American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals)

items.text: Long-haired breeds will need a little help, particularly Persians, who have a very thick undercoat and a long top layer of fur.
Scratching posts placed around your home let your cat scratch naturally, help limit damage to furniture and support healthy claws.

Always keep a constant supply of fresh, clean water available. Cats fed mainly dry food tend not to drink enough on their own, so several water stations, ceramic or steel bowls, or a fountain can encourage drinking.
items.sourceName: Should I feed my cat wet or dry food?

items.text: Cats evolved in dry regions and respond to low-moisture food by concentrating their urine rather than drinking more, which is one reason moisture-rich wet food can help hydration.
items.sourceName: Should I feed my cat wet or dry food?
